alternative: Derive from both parents directly - class Ball : public GameItem, public Thread - and declare the shared base virtual when the hierarchy is diamond-shaped; disambiguate the rare name clash with using-declarations. Keep the two hierarchies independent by composing two members and forwarding explicitly, or use CRTP/template mixins when the second parent is a static policy. The twin's two-object structure only adds a second allocation, a mutual reference and lifetime questions.
idiom_name: pair of derived classes with a mutual reference (unnecessary where multiple inheritance is available)
implementation_notes: C++ derives a class from any number of base classes, so the capability the twin imitates is a language feature: cppreference states that 'any class type (whether declared with class-key class or struct) may be declared as derived from one or more base classes', and a diamond is handled by declaring the shared base virtual so that the most derived object holds one subobject of it. The same reference documents member name lookup with the rules of dominance and using-declarations for the residual ambiguities, which is exactly what the twin avoids by splitting the object - but at the price of a second object, a cycle and manual forwarding. What replaces the twin link: real multiple inheritance, or composition of two members with explicit forwarding when the two parents must stay independent, or template mixins/CRTP when the second parent is a compile-time policy. A twin pair is still defensible in a codebase that forbids multiple inheritance by convention or when one parent is not designable for multiple inheritance (a framework base with non-virtual destructors), and then the pair should be composed of two members with one-way forwarding rather than a mutual cycle.
pitfalls: Non-virtual multiple inheritance duplicates a shared base subobject and its state; a common grandparent must be declared virtual or the two parts of the hierarchy see different copies.
Members present in both bases are ambiguous at the call site and must be disambiguated (Base::member or a using-declaration) - a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
Constructor and destructor order follows the base-clause order, so members that must be initialised before the other base's constructor runs need an explicit design.

Virtual bases add indirection and move virtual-base initialisation to the most derived class, which makes base constructors with arguments awkward; a framework base not designed for it (non-virtual destructor) must not be used polymorphically.
